parts.title: Viking Ireland
parts.article:
A When Irish archaeologists working under Dublin’s South Great George’s Street unearthed the remains of four young men buried with fragments of Viking shields, daggers and personal ornaments, the excavation appeared to be simply more evidence of the Viking presence in Ireland. At least 77 Viking burial sites have been found across Dublin since the late 18th century. All have been dated to the ninth or tenth centuries on the basis of artefacts that accompanied them, and the South Great George’s Street burials seemed to be further examples. Yet when archaeologist Linzi Simpson sent the remains for analysis, the tests showed that the men had been buried in Irish soil years, or even decades, before the accepted date for the establishment of the first year-round Viking settlement in Dublin.

B Simpson’s findings are now adding new weight to an idea gaining growing acceptance – that instead of a sudden, calamitous invasion, the arrival of the Vikings in Ireland started with small-scale settlements and trade links that connected Ireland with northern Europe. And, further, that those trading contacts may have occurred generations before the violent raids described in contemporary texts, works written by monks living in isolated monasteries. These were often the only places where literate people lived and were especially targeted by Viking raiders for their food supplies and treasures. Scholars are continuing to examine the texts written by monks, but are also considering the limitations of using them. ‘Most researchers accept now that the raids were not the first contact, as the old texts suggest,’ says Viking expert Gareth Williams. ‘How did the Vikings know where all those monasteries were? It’s because there was already contact. They were already trading before those raids happened.’

C Although the earlier dates for a Viking presence in Dublin that have been identified by Simpson and independent archaeologists differ from the later dates by only a few decades, when combined with other evidence, they are challenging the chronology of Viking settlement in Ireland. Since the 1960s, archaeologists have been gathering information about the mid-ninth-century settlement that lay under the sidewalks of Fishamble Street in Dublin. According to archaeologist Ruth Johnson, the Vikings started with sporadic summer raids, but after some years of profitable plunder, they decided to stay, and built settlements for the winter.

D Carbon dating, which measures the age of organic materials based on the amount of radioactive carbon-14 remaining in a specimen, usually gives a range of likely dates for the time of death. The older the material, the wider the range. In the case of the four individuals excavated at the South Great George’s Street site, Simpson found that two of them had a 95 per cent probability of having died between 670 and 880, with a 68 per cent probability of death occurring between 690 and 790. Thus, the entire most likely range was before the first documented arrival of Vikings in 795. A third individual lived slightly later, with a 95 per cent probability of having died between 689 and 882. The dates were not what Simpson had thought they would be. ‘These dates seem impossibly early and difficult to reconcile with the available historical and archaeological sources,’ she says.

E The fourth individual excavated at South Great George’s Street was the most intact of the group, and revealed the most about the lives and hardships of Vikings at this time. A powerfully built man in his late teens or early 20s, he was approximately 1.70m tall by the day’s standards, with the muscular torso and upper limbs that would have come from hard, ocean-going rowing. His bones showed stresses associated with heavy lifting beginning in childhood. Unlike the three other men, he was not buried with weapons. Like one of the other men found at the burial site, he had a congenital deformity at the base of his spine, perhaps indicating they were relatives. Carbon dating gave a wider range for his lifetime, showing a 95 per cent probability that he died between 786 and 955.

F Tests were also carried out on the four South Great George’s Street men’s isotopic oxygen levels. Such tests indicate where a person spent their childhood based on a chemical signature left by groundwater in developing teeth. The results showed that the two men with the spinal deformity had spent their childhood in Scandinavia. However, the other two had spent their childhoods in Ireland or Scotland, another sign of permanent settlement by Viking families and not just summertime raids by warriors.

G The evidence of an earlier-than-expected Viking presence in Ireland, based as it is on forensic tests conducted on a handful of burial sites, may seem slight. But seemingly small pieces of evidence can overturn well-established conventions in archaeology. Both Simpson and Johnson stress that more excavations and tests will be needed before anyone can rewrite the history of Viking settlement, and such work is years away. Williams adds, ‘There are two possibilities raised by [Simpson’s] work. Either there was Viking activity earlier than we’ve realised in Ireland, or there is something in the water or soil in Dublin skewing the data, and both possibilities need further research.’ Nevertheless, Williams agrees with Simpson and others that the chronology of the Viking presence in Ireland is uncertain, and that they were possibly trading or raiding in Ireland before 795. ‘It’s a poorly documented part of history,’ says Williams. ‘But before there was Viking settlement, there was this big trading zone in the North Sea. Did it extend to the Irish Sea? We don’t have any evidence to say that, but it could be just a question of time.’

Q14

解析 A段前半部分提到一开始这些墓地被认为是9世纪或10世纪的常规遗址，但后面的化验结果推翻了这个结论，证明下葬时间要早得多。

干扰 你可能看到第一句的挖掘（unearthed）就想选有关地址的选项，但这几句话的核心转折其实在于“本以为是常规的旧遗址，检测却发现不是”。

句子 All have been dated to the ninth or tenth centuries on the basis of artefacts that accompanied them, and the South Great George’s Street burials seemed to be further examples. Yet when archaeologist Linzi Simpson sent the remains for analysis, the tests showed that the men had been buried in Irish soil years, or even decades, before the accepted date for the establishment of the first year-round Viking settlement in Dublin.

Q15

解析 B段明确指出学者们正在反思由僧侣所写旧文献的局限性，并认为旧文献中关于“第一次接触就是袭击”的记载是不对的。

干扰 你可能会因为提到了贸易（trading）而去寻找关于商业或经济的选项，但本段的核心其实是质疑并推翻了旧史料里的传统说法。

句子 Scholars are continuing to examine the texts written by monks, but are also considering the limitations of using them. ‘Most researchers accept now that the raids were not the first contact, as the old texts suggest,’ says Viking expert Gareth Williams.

Q16

解析 C段最后一句话直接点出维京人经过几年的掠夺后“决定留下来过冬（decided to stay）”，这完美对应了选项里的较长时期留在爱尔兰。

干扰 你可能看到前面的“夏季袭击（summer raids）”感到迷惑，但重点在于紧随其后的转折——他们随后改变主意选择了长久定居。

句子 According to archaeologist Ruth Johnson, the Vikings started with sporadic summer raids, but after some years of profitable plunder, they decided to stay, and built settlements for the winter.

Q17

解析 D段详细介绍了一种叫做“碳年代测定法（Carbon dating）”的研究技术，而整段的核心在于测出来的年份出乎意料得早，与预期完全不符。

干扰 你可能()光看各种数字觉得这段只是在罗列时间，但整段的主线是这个测定技术带来了一个让人大跌眼镜的意外结果。

句子 Carbon dating, which measures the age of organic materials based on the amount of radioactive carbon-14 remaining in a specimen, usually gives a range of likely dates for the time of death. The older the material, the wider the range. Thus, the entire most likely range was before the first documented arrival of Vikings in 795. A third individual lived slightly later, with a 95 per cent probability of having died between 689 and 882. The dates were not what Simpson had thought they would be. ‘These dates seem impossibly early and difficult to reconcile with the available historical and archaeological sources,’ she says.

Q18

解析 E段一上来就说这具骨架揭示了这名维京人的“生活与艰辛”，后面紧接着详细描述了他因为长期划船和从小干重活而形成的独特身体特征。

干扰 你可能看到骨骼畸形（congenital deformity）想找健康或疾病相关的选项，但本段从身高、肌肉到干苦力，都在完整勾勒这一个特定维京人的生活方式。

句子 The fourth individual excavated at South Great George’s Street was the most intact of the group, and revealed the most about the lives and hardships of Vikings at this time. A powerfully built man in his late teens or early 20s, he was approximately 1.70m tall by the day’s standards, with the muscular torso and upper limbs that wo()uld have come from hard, ocea()n-going rowing. His bones showed stresses associated with heavy lifting beginning in childhood.

Q19

解析 F段通过同位素测试，明确测出了这几个人是在哪里度过童年的（比如斯堪的纳维亚、爱尔兰或苏格兰），直接对应选项里的“成长地点”。

干扰 这段虽然提到了化验（Tests），但落脚点全在具体的地名和“度过童年（spent their childhood）”上，千万不要跟D段的碳定年法搞混选了vi。

The results showed that the two men with the spinal deformity had spent their childhood in Scandinavia. However, the other two had spent their childhoods in Ireland or Scotland, another sign of permanent settlement by Viking families and not just summertime raids by warriors.

Q20

解析 G段中几位专家反复强调，在改写历史之前，我们需要“更多的挖掘和测试（more excavations and tests）”以及“进一步的研究（further research）”。

干扰 你可能看到()段落末尾提到的贸易区（trading zone）而分心，但全段的核心观点是目前的证据还太单薄，必须要有更多补充数据支撑才能下定论。

句子 Both Simpson and Johnson s()tress that more excavations and tests will be needed before anyone can rewrite the history of Viking settlement, and such work is years away. Williams adds, ‘There are two possibilities raised by [Simpson’s] work. Either there was Viking activity earlier than we’ve realised in Ireland, or there is something in the water or soil in Dublin skewing the data, and both possibilities need further research.’

Q21

解析 原文明确指出露丝·约翰逊（Ruth Johnson）认为，维京人是在经历了几年“有利可图的掠夺（profitable plunder）”后决定留下来的，指的就是经济利益带来的好处)。

干扰 你可能不认识plunder（掠夺）或者觉得它不完全等于financial benefits（经济利益），但profitable（有利可图的）直接帮你锁定了这层金钱上的好处。

句子 According to archaeologist Ruth Johnson, the Vikings started with sporadic summer raids, but after some years of profitable plunder, they decided to stay, and built settlements for the winter.

Q22

解析 林齐·辛普森（Linzi Simpson）发现测出的年份与她的预期大相径庭，且这些日子早得难以和现有的史料相吻合，这完美对应了数据不一致带来的惊讶。

干扰 不要只要看到数据（data）就去选提到了测试数据的其他专家，这里强调的是数据与现有事实“难以调和（difficult to reconcile）”的意外感。

句子 The dates were not what Simpson had thought they would be. ‘These dates seem impossibly early and difficult to reconcile with the available historical and archaeological sources,’ she says

Q23

解析 加雷斯·威廉姆斯（Gareth Williams）提出了一种可能性，即都柏林的“水或土壤（water or soil）”中可能有什么物质使得数据发生了倾斜，这对应的就是受到地质因素的影响。

干扰 你可能会错过“水或土壤（water or soil）”与“地质因素（geological factors）”之间的同义替换，要注意专家在探讨化验偏差时具体的猜想对象。

句子 Williams adds, ‘There are two possibilities raised by [Simpson’s] work. Either there was Viking activity earlier than we’ve realised in Ireland, or there is something in the water or soil in Dublin skewing the data, and both possibilities need further research.’

Q24

解析 原文直接提到这个人的身高按“当时的标准（by the day's standards）”来看大约是1.70米，因此填入standards。

干扰 注意一定要完全照抄原文的词汇形式，不要把复数结尾的“s”漏掉。

句子 A powerfully built man in his late teens or early 20s, he was approximately 1.70m tall by the day’s standards, with the muscular torso and upper limbs that would have come from hard, ocean-going rowing.

Q25

解析 原文说他骨骼上因干重活留下的劳损是从“童年时期（childhood）”开始的，刚好对应题目中的“追溯到他的（dated from his）...”。

干扰 题干的dated from（追溯到）对应了原文的beginning in（开始于），只要锁定stresses（劳损）就能往后找到对应的人生阶段。

句子 His bones showed stresses associated with heavy lifting beginning in childhood.

Q26

解析 题目问的是他的下部哪里有基因异常（genetic abnormality），原文明确写着他在“脊柱的底部（base of his spine）”有先天畸形，对应lower spine，因此填spine。

干扰 你可能不认识congenital deformity（先天畸形），但是看到base（底部）对应题干的lower（下部），就能直接精准定位到后面的spine（脊柱）。

句子 Like one of the other men found at the burial site, he had a congenital deformity at the base of his spine, perhaps indicating they were relatives.
